Whether it's clothing, beer, food, or just a roadside repair kit, there is a surprising variety in the ways you can carry stuff on a bike.

* Backpack. For the average person, this is the most accessible way to start carrying things on a bicycle. You probably have a backpack already, and it doesn't require you to do anything except pack it up and put it on. The problem is that wearing a loaded backpack on a bicycle can be torturous. It puts strain on your back, can make you sweat horribly, and it throws off your balance. If you're going to wear a backpack on a bicycle, it probably shouldn't be any bigger than a camelbak, and you probably shouldn't put too much weight in it. You can also buy special backpacks for cycling, but they're often expensive and not superior enough to a normal backpack to justify the cost in my personal view. If you can make a backpack work for you, then more power to you, but there are much better options of you are willing to invest a little time and money. * Hip bag (a.k.a. "fanny pack" in the U.S.). While some of these are quite large, the average one won't be able to carry a whole lot. They're good to carry a mini pump, wallet, keys, phone, spare tube, patch kit, CO2, multitool/levers, and maybe a couple energy bars. The advantage they have is that they allow you to carry things lower on your body than a backpack. It's like a poor man's cycling jersey (cycle jerseys have pockets in the back in roughly the same area as a hip bag would go, and can carry all the items listed above). * Saddle bag. These clip on under the back of your bike saddle. Most are small and only meant to carry your common roadside repair items (spare tube, multitool, tire levers, patch kit, CO2), but you can get larger ones if you want to carry more. * Frame bags. This is a blanket term for various zipper bags that strap on to your bike frame, usually with velcro. They are expensive and usually can't carry a whole lot. Probably the most common type is a triangle frame bag. It gets its name from the fact that it fits inside the large front triangle of the bike frame. These aren't worth the money IMO. While a full set of frame bags can be used for light bicycle touring, they cost too much and simply don't carry enough. The reason they cost so much is that bike geometry varies so much from bike to bike, so frame bags are typically made as specialty items for a specific model of bike only. The advantage they have is in allowing you to carry stuff while keeping the aerodynamic profile of your bike low, and the bags themselves usually don't add a lot of weight. They are an expensive option for people with expensive bikes. * Rear rack. There are two main types of rear rack. One type attaches directly to the bike, and the other clamps onto the seatpost. A seatpost rack is inferior, but has its uses. Seatpost racks, which often have a quick release so they can be easily taken on and off the bike, are good if you're unable to mount a normal rack to your frame. A seatpost rack will not be very stable. It will want to swivel from side to side, can't carry as much weight as a normal rack, and usually can't be used with a full size set of rear panniers. In my opinion, racks are the best thing to have on a bike if you want to carry stuff. As soon as you have at least a rear rack, your options for carrying things open up significantly. You can:

----------

1. Strap stuff to the top of it with bungies. Some people even strap their backpacks to it. 1. Attach a basket or milk crate onto it by using zip ties or a couple of gear ties. Milk crates are so great! They're sturdy and spacious enough easily carry a load of groceries. Hook a small cargo net over the top to prevent stuff from flying out if you hit a bump or tip the bike over. Hardware stores like Home Depot actually sell milk crates, so you don't have an excuse to go out and steal one. Don't do that. Bike shops often also sell bike cargo nets. 1. Attach side baskets. There are baskets designed to hang off the sides of rear racks. Some types can even fold up when not in use. Check your local bike shop for these. Just check to make sure you have enough heel clearance to pedal the bike when the baskets are unfolded. Some bikes won't have enough room. 1. Put a trunk bag on it. A trunk bag is a large pannier that sits on top of your rear rack, and some are even able to deploy small side panniers that hang down over the sides of the rack for even more storage room. 1. Put a set of rear panniers on it. A full size set of rear panniers is a beautiful thing! They can carry so much, and since the weight is carried lower on the bike, it's better for balance. They can be pretty spendy, but IMO they are definitely worth every penny.

----------

* Front basket. These are okay, but since they attach to your handlebars, they really affect your steering, especially when loaded. Any weight you put on the front of a bike should be as close to the front axle as possible. The higher it is, the more difficult it makes controlling the bike. IMO you should hook a cargo net over the top to prevent stuff from flying out of a fully loaded one. Baskets you can take off quickly are best. * Handlebar bag. It's like a front basket, but not as heavy, not as big, and is able to protect items inside. There are two types: the kind that goes on with straps (usually velcro), and the kind that goes on with a quick release clip. The clip style is better, but costs more. Handlebar bags are for storing your phone, wallet, keys, and anything else small that you might need quick access to while riding, such as snacks or a camera. They usually also have a transparent map case on the top so you can potentially read a map without stopping. * Front rack. There are 3 main types of front racks. Platform, lowrider, and a combination of the first two. Front platforms are for strapping stuff to the top of like you would on a rear rack, and some will also have the correct geometry for side panniers. You can also attach a basket or a trunk bag on it. Lowriders are specifically for attaching front panniers to the left and right sides of your fork as low down as possible to minimize difficulty in steering the bike with added weight in the front. And then a full front rack will just allow both low pannier attachment and also have a platform over the wheel.

As extensive as this list is, I'm sure I've left stuff out. I just wanted to let people know that there are lots of ways to carry things on a bike, which means using them for commuting or running errands or even going on a holiday are all totally viable options.
